summary: Explains why peer-to-peer and other distributed applications can waste network resources by choosing peers without knowing the network layout. It sets out the problem Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) should solve: giving applications guidance about better choices. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Distributed applications often choose a source or peer without knowing how the network connects to it. This RFC describes a service that could provide network guidance to help applications choose more effectively.

questions: why do p2p applications need network topology information
why do p2p applications waste bandwidth

subtitle: Why distributed applications need guidance when choosing among network peers.

tldr.problem: Distributed applications often choose peers without reliable information about the network paths beneath them, which can create inefficient traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes an information-sharing service that provides slowly changing network guidance so applications can make better-than-random peer choices.
tldr.outcome: This is a problem statement, not a protocol or requirements specification. It identifies use cases and design issues including privacy and topology information.

today: RFC 5693 is an Informational problem statement published in October 2009. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Peer Selection Matters
sections.content:
File sharing, media streaming, and other distributed applications may have several peers that can provide the same resource. Applications often choose randomly or rely on partial measurements, such as connection setup time, that do not reliably show the throughput of later data transfer.

These choices can send traffic across network boundaries and load links that are already congested. The RFC describes ALTO as a way for an application to obtain network information and use it when selecting endpoints.
sections.plainLanguage: An application may have several places to get the same file or service. Information about the underlying network can help it choose among them instead of relying only on a random choice or limited measurements.

sections.title: The ALTO Client and Server
sections.content:
An ALTO client sends a query to an ALTO server, and the server replies with guidance. The client can be part of the application that needs a resource, part of a directory that lists providers, or both. A query and its response form an ALTO transaction.

The RFC limits the ALTO client protocol to those queries and responses. The application protocol between peers and the provisioning protocol that supplies information to the server are outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: An ALTO client asks an ALTO server for guidance, and the server returns information that can help choose a provider. The RFC’s scope is this exchange, not the application’s data transfer.

sections.title: Where Guidance Could Be Used
sections.content:
The RFC describes five use cases: file sharing, cache or mirror selection, live media streaming, real-time communications, and distributed hash tables. In each case, an application or directory may have several possible sources, peers, or relays to choose from.

For example, a file-sharing application can use guidance to rank sources for a file, while a streaming application can use it to select peers that exchange media. A real-time communication application may use it to choose among media relays.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed guidance could help choose file sources, download mirrors, streaming peers, or communication relays. These are examples of where an application can make an early choice among several possible endpoints.

sections.title: Information, Trust, and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC says ALTO is better suited to information that changes slowly, such as operator policies, geographical location, network proximity, transmission costs, or traffic quotas. Rapidly changing conditions such as transport congestion are better measured by the applications themselves.

Network operators, third parties, or user communities could provide the service. Applications may not want to reveal their type, and operators may not want to disclose network topology. The RFC also notes that an ALTO provider could influence application choices, so a design should not assume that clients or servers must reveal sensitive information.
sections.plainLanguage: ALTO guidance is most useful for facts that change slowly, not moment-by-moment congestion. A design also needs to respect that applications and network operators may want to keep some information private.
